verses.6:2: Senhor, não me {arguas} no vosso furor, * nem me {corripias} na vossa ira.
verses.6:3: Tende piedade de mim, Senhor, porque {infirmus}: * {sana}, Senhor, porque os meus ossos {conturbata}.
verses.6:4: E a minha alma {turbata}: * mas vós, Senhor, até quando?
verses.6:5: {convertere}, Senhor, e {eripe} a minha alma: * salvai-me por causa da vossa misericórdia.
verses.6:6: Porque na morte não há quem se lembre de vós: * {inferno}, porém, quem vos {confitebitur}?
verses.6:7: {laboravi}, † lavarei {singulas} {lectum}: * com as minhas lágrimas regarei {stratum}.
verses.6:8: O meu olho {turbatus} {afurore}: * envelheci entre todos os meus inimigos.
verses.6:9: {discedite} de mim, todos vós que praticais a iniquidade: * porque o Senhor {exaudivit} a voz do meu pranto.
verses.6:10: O Senhor {exaudivit} a minha {deprecationem}, * o Senhor {suscepit} a minha oração.

decisions.latin: ne in furóre tuo árguas me
decisions.why: The opening of the first Penitential Psalm, and word for word the opening of the third (37:2) — what is ruled here is ruled for both. árguere has five verses (6:2, 37:2, 49:8, 49:21, 93:10; grep) and stands in one verse with corrípere three times; the Greek is ἐλέγχω, to reprove, to convict. Lewis & Short: with a person, 'to accuse, reprove, censure, charge with', quoting the Digest: 'arguisse accusasse et convicisse'. The natural Portuguese word, 'repreender', is the glossary's word for increpáre (ἐπιτιμάω — another Greek verb; twelve verses, 118:21 already translated), which meets corrípere in 140:5.

options.label: não me repreendais
options.note: Draft 3, ruled by the main session (DECISIONS.md D21). Every living witness says rebuke: Douay-Rheims, the Diurnal (‘não me repreendas’); Matos Soares 1932 keeps the cognate, which is dead. The Greek pair ἐλέγχω … παιδεύω is reproof and chastening, what a father does; ‘acusar’ makes God the prosecutor in a verse where he is the judge, and takes one sense of árguere where the Latin holds several. The word is shared with increpáre (working, one verse so far): the two never stand in one verse of the psalter (checked with ps005/grep_latin.py), and they are different Greek verbs, so a reader crossing columns loses that distinction. Cost also named by the agent: ‘repreendais’ has a hiatus before the stress. No critic has read draft 3.

options.label: não me acuseis
options.note: Draft 2’s wording, by the translating agent. The verb's own sense in Lewis & Short, a plain word, free in the glossary (accusáre does not occur in the psalter — grep), and the right one for the other places: 49:21 árguam te, et státuam contra fáciem tuam ('eu te acusarei, e porei tudo diante da tua face'), 49:8. The verse then moves from charge to penalty: não me acuseis … nem me castigueis. It is easy in the mouth, where 're-pre-en-dais' has a hiatus at the stress. Proposed for the glossary.

options.label: não me arguais
options.note: Matos Soares 1932 ('Não me arguas'). The cognate; in Brazil 'arguir' is to examine a candidate, and the form is not heard as anything.

options.label: não me censureis
options.note: Lewis & Short's 'censure'. Too slight: it is what a critic does.

decisions.latin: neque in ira tua corrípias me
decisions.why: corrípere has seven verses (6:2, 37:2, 38:12, 89:10, 93:10, 104:14, 140:5). The Greek is παιδεύω — the same verb that stands behind castigáre in 117:18 (παιδεύων ἐπαίδευσεν; checked in consult/parallels/ps117.md), which the glossary renders 'castigar'. castigáre has no other verse in the psalter (the noun once, 72:14) and never meets corrípere. 'Corrigir' would say the sense well but belongs to corrígere (17:36b, 95:10, 118:9).

options.label: nem me castigueis
options.note: Ruling: Matos Soares 1932 ('nem me castigues'), Douay-Rheims 'chastise', the Diurnal. It shares the word with castigáre on D15's test — one Greek verb, and the two Latin verbs never stand together. It serves the other places (140:5 'O justo me castigará com misericórdia'; 38:12 'castigastes o homem'). Proposed for the glossary.

options.label: nem me corrijais
options.note: Nearer the Greek's 'discipline'; it is corrígere's word, and 'corrijais' is a hard form to sing.

options.label: nem me repreendais
options.note: corrípere can be 'reprove' in classical Latin; here the Greek decides for chastening, and the word is increpáre's.

decisions.why: infírmus is 'not firm': weak, and sick (the Greek ἀσθενής has both). The verse goes on 'sana me', which leans to sickness; the family in the psalter leans to weakness (infirmáti sunt et cecidérunt 26:2, génua mea infirmáta sunt 108:24), but 102:3 has 'qui sanat omnes infirmitátes tuas'. The Latin adjective is masculine, and Portuguese cannot avoid a gender here either.

options.label: porque estou enfermo
options.note: Ruling: the cognate (Matos Soares 1932 'sou enfermo'), which answers 'curai-me' in the next colon as infírmus answers sana. 'Estou', because it is a state he asks to be healed of. Cost: 'enfermo' no longer says weakness, which infírmus also says.

options.label: porque estou fraco
options.note: Douay-Rheims 'weak'. The family's usual sense (enfraquecer will be wanted for infirmári); loses the link with sana.

options.label: porque sou enfermo
options.note: Matos Soares 1932 exactly. 'Sou' makes it a condition of nature — a possible reading (man's frailty), but it sits badly with 'curai-me'.

decisions.why: sanáre has seven verses (6:3, 29:3, 40:5 sana ánimam meam, 59:4, 102:3, 106:20, 146:3). Both Portuguese verbs are safe at the vós imperative (curai / sarai; pasts curei / sarei).

options.label: curai-me
options.note: Ruling: the plain living verb (D2: of two faithful words the plainer), the Diurnal's ('cura-me'); it takes any object the psalter gives it ('curai a minha alma', 'que cura todas as tuas enfermidades'). Proposed for the glossary.

options.label: sarai-me
options.note: Matos Soares 1932 ('sara-me'). The verb of the same root as sanáre; in Brazil 'sarar' is mostly what the patient does ('sarou'), and the transitive is old.

options.label: sanai-me
options.note: The cognate; 'sanar' is to remedy a defect or a debt.

decisions.latin: conturbáta sunt ossa mea … ánima mea turbáta est valde … Turbátus est … óculus meus … conturbéntur veheménter omnes inimíci mei
decisions.why: The psalm is built on one verb four times: my bones, my soul, my eye are troubled — let my enemies be troubled. The Latin varies only the prefix (con-turbáre / turbáre); the Greek has ταράσσω all four times. The glossary has turbáre → perturbar (working, Ps 118:60) and conturbáre → perturbar (open, Ps 2:5), with the note 'to be tried on Ps 6 (conturbáta sunt ossa mea)'. This is that trial. The trouble: bones and an eye that are 'perturbados' are strange Portuguese — as ossa conturbáta and óculus turbátus are strange Latin.

options.label: perturbar, four times
options.note: Ruling. D2 keeps the Latin's repetitions, and this one is the psalm's frame: what has happened to me is asked upon them. One glossary verb for both Latin verbs, as the Greek has one. The perfect passives are read as the state that results (Douay-Rheims 'are troubled … is troubled'), beside the present 'infírmus sum'. The strangeness of troubled bones and a troubled eye is the Latin's and stays (rule 2).

options.label: perturbar, but the eye 'se turvou'
options.note: What Portuguese says of an eye (Matos Soares 1932 'Os meus olhos se turbaram'): turbátus as clouded. Natural, and of the same Latin root; breaks one link of the chain and settles that the eye is dimmed rather than troubled.

options.label: abalar, four times
options.note: The Diurnal's verb for the bones and the enemies ('abalado … abalados'). Good of bones and soul, impossible of an eye; and it is commovére's natural word (non commovébitur).

options.label: as Matos Soares: estremeceram … turbou-se … se turvou … conturbados
options.note: Matos Soares 1932, four renderings for the one verb. Each is apt in its place; the psalm's frame is gone. 'Conturbar' failed both blind readers in Ps 2.

decisions.why: The same verb at both ends of the prayer: 'Turn, Lord' (6:5) and 'let them be turned' (6:11). The glossary has convértere → voltar (open, Ps 118:59, 79), because 'converter' is heard as religious conversion, and names 'Convérte nos, Deus' as a place it must serve. Convértere, Dómine returns in 89:13 (with úsquequo, as here in 6:4–5) and 79:15. In 6:11 the Latin does not say 'back' (69:4 does: avertántur retrórsum), so convertántur is open between being turned back in flight and being turned, converted.

options.label: Voltai-vos … voltem-se
options.note: Ruling: the glossary verb at both ends, so the echo is heard; safe at the vós imperative (past 'voltei'); Matos Soares 1932 has 'Volta-te' in 6:5. In 6:11 nothing is added: 'voltem-se' leaves them to turn away or to turn round, as the Latin does. Cost: the second colon of 6:11 is five syllables short. Heard: the blind reader listed all three readings of 'voltem-se' (retreat, turn to God, merely turn round) — the Latin's own range — with retreat first.

options.label: Voltai-vos … voltem atrás
options.note: Douay-Rheims 'let them be turned back', Matos Soares 1932 'retirem-se'. Adds the 'back' that the Latin keeps for 69:4, and closes the reading of conversion.

options.label: Convertei-vos … convertam-se
options.note: The cognate. 'Convertei-vos, Senhor' asks God to repent.

decisions.why: The glossary has erípere → arrancar (open, Ps 90:15, 53:9), kept apart from liberáre → livrar. It was made on places that name what one is snatched from, or have a person as object ('Arrancai-me'). Here the object is 'my soul' and no source is named — the only such éripe of the seventeen in the psalter (grep) — and 'arrancai a minha alma' says in Portuguese 'tear out my soul', which is to kill.

options.label: libertai a minha alma
options.note: Ruling for this verse: the alternative the glossary row itself names, the Diurnal's verb ('liberta a minha alma'); still apart from liberáre → livrar, safe at the imperative (past 'libertei'). The snatching is lost. Reported to the glossary: arrancar fails where the object is 'a minha alma' and no 'de' follows.

options.label: arrancai a minha alma
options.note: The glossary verb. Refused here: without a 'de …' it is heard as tearing the soul out.

options.label: livrai a minha alma
options.note: Matos Soares 1932 ('livra a minha alma'), Douay-Rheims 'deliver'. It is liberáre's word, and 58:2, 68:15, 70:1, 143:7 set éripe and líbera side by side.

options.label: arrebatai a minha alma
options.note: Keeps the snatching; heard as 'take my soul away' — the opposite of what is asked.

decisions.why: inférnus is the world of the dead (the Greek ᾅδης), parallel here to 'in morte'; nineteen verses have inférnus / ínferi (grep), among them 15:10 non derelínques ánimam meam in inférno and 138:8 si descéndero in inférnum, ades. In Portuguese 'inferno' is first the hell of the damned. Douay-Rheims keeps 'hell'; Matos Soares paraphrases ('na habitação dos mortos'); the Diurnal has 'nos limbos'.

options.label: no inferno
options.note: Ruling: the Latin's word (D2), which a Latin ear also heard as hell; in this verse both senses are true — neither the dead nor the damned give thanks. It names a place with one plain word, as the Latin does, and it keeps the psalm penitential. Proposed for the glossary as `open`: 15:10 and 138:8 are the places that will test it hardest.

options.label: nos infernos
options.note: The plural is the old Portuguese name for the abode of the dead, as distinct from 'o inferno' (the Creed's 'desceu aos infernos' — from memory, unverified). Changes the Latin's number and is no longer current.

options.label: na mansão dos mortos
options.note: The phrase of the Creed as now said in Brazil (from memory, unverified). Three words for one, a second 'mort-' the Latin does not have, and an explanation (rule 2).

options.label: na habitação dos mortos
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. The same objections.

decisions.why: D5: confitéri to God → dar graças a. This verse is one of its tests: the verb stands parallel to 'memor sit tui', and Matos Soares and the Diurnal both write 'louvará'.

options.label: quem vos dará graças?
options.note: D5, applied — and it holds: the dative is kept ('vos'), the question is as natural as 'quem vos louvará', and it closes the colon on the paroxytone 'graças'. Remembering and giving thanks go together (the Greek ἐξομολογήσεται).

options.label: quem vos louvará?
options.note: Matos Soares 1932, the Diurnal. It is laudáre's verb (D5).

options.label: quem vos confessará?
options.note: Douay-Rheims 'confess to thee'. In Portuguese, to profess faith in God or to hear his confession (D5).

decisions.why: laboráre is to toil and to be worn by toil; the Greek (ἐκοπίασα) says 'I grew weary'. 68:4 has the twin: Laborávi clamans. gémitus is singular (eight verses; → gemido). 'Cansei-me de gemer' would say 'I am fed up with groaning', which is not the sense. Draft 1 had 'Cansei-me no meu gemido'; the stylist heard a translated preposition and asked for 'Cansei-me de gemer'.

options.label: Cansei-me gemendo
options.note: Draft 2. The stylist's point taken — 'cansar-se em' + noun is not said — but not his wording: a gerund is how Brazilian Portuguese says what one wore oneself out doing, it adds nothing, and it cannot be heard as 'I am fed up with'. A noun turned into a verb form is grammar (D2, as D16 did with elóquium). Cost: 'meo' is no longer said, and 68:4 Laborávi clamans will have the same build though the Latin differs.

options.label: Cansei-me de gemer
options.note: The stylist's own wording. Refused: 'cansei-me de' + infinitive is first of all 'I have had enough of' (cansei-me de esperar) — a sense the Latin does not have; Matos Soares needed 'de tanto gemer' to steer away from it.

options.label: Cansei-me no meu gemido
options.note: Draft 1: the perfect, the Greek's weariness, the Latin's 'in' and its singular noun. Refused by the stylist: 'a preposição deixa a frase pouco natural na boca'.

options.label: Fatiguei-me no meu gemido
options.note: Same sense, one syllable more, a shade more bookish.

options.label: Labutei no meu gemido
options.note: Douay-Rheims 'I have laboured'. The toil without the weariness.

options.label: Estou esgotado de tanto gemer
options.note: Matos Soares 1932 ('Estou esgotado à força de tanto gemer'). A present and a paraphrase.

decisions.why: A distributive plural: night by night, every single night.

options.label: todas as noites
options.note: Ruling: keeps the plural (the glossary keeps the plural of noctes in 133:2); Matos Soares 1932.

options.label: cada noite
options.note: Says síngulas better and is shorter; singular (the Diurnal: 'cada noite').

options.label: noite após noite
options.note: The distributive as a figure; a touch literary.

decisions.why: Two words for the bed in one verse (Greek κλίνη / στρωμνή), and the psalter has a third, cubíle, which Ps 4:5 rendered 'leito'. lectus and stratum meet again in 40:4 and, as one phrase, in 131:3 (in lectum strati mei); 62:7 has stratum alone. Portuguese has two plain words.

options.label: o meu leito … a minha cama
options.note: Ruling: the two plain words in the Diurnal's order ('o leito … a cama'), so that the verse has two as the Latin has. lectus shares 'leito' with cubíle (they never meet). 40:4 follows easily ('sobre o leito da sua dor … toda a sua cama'); 131:3 lectum strati mei cannot ('o leito da minha cama') and will decide locally. Proposed for the glossary.

options.label: a minha cama … o meu leito
options.note: The other way round: lectus as the everyday word. Then stratum shares 'leito' with cubíle; the verse falls from the plain word to the literary one.

options.label: o meu leito … o lugar do meu descanso
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. A paraphrase of stratum.

decisions.latin: Turbátus est a furóre óculus meus
decisions.why: Whose fury? The Latin has no possessive. It is the word of 6:2 (in furóre tuo), so it can be God's fury that troubles the eye; the Greek θυμός can also be the sufferer's own passion (the Hebrew has 'grief'). Douay-Rheims: 'through indignation'. Portuguese must choose between an article and none. furor → furor (glossary).

options.label: pelo furor
options.note: Ruling: 'a' + ablative of the agent or cause → 'por'. With the article the hearer may think back to 'vosso furor' of the first verse, as the Latin's repeated word invites, but is not made to.

options.label: de furor
options.note: Without the article it is the speaker's own fury. Closes the link with 6:2.

options.label: por causa do furor
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. Same openness, three syllables more; 'por causa de' is kept for propter.

decisions.latin: Discédite a me, omnes, qui operámini iniquitátem
decisions.why: discédere, to go away (ἀπόστητε); the imperative only here in the psalter. The glossary has declináre a → apartar-se de (118:115 Declináte a me, malígni → 'Apartai-vos de mim') and amovére / repéllere → afastar (transitive). The Gospel quotes this line (Mt 7:23 — from memory, unverified).

options.label: Afastai-vos de mim
options.note: Ruling: the Diurnal's word for word ('Afastai-vos de mim, todos os que praticais o mal'); the reflexive of a verb the glossary already has; safe (past 'afastei'). It stays apart from 118:115 'Apartai-vos'.

options.label: Retirai-vos de mim
options.note: A verb of its own for discédere, safe too; more polite than the Latin.

options.label: Apartai-vos de mim
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. It is declináre's in the glossary (118:115, a near twin of this line).

decisions.latin: exaudívit Dóminus vocem fletus mei. Exaudívit Dóminus deprecatiónem meam
decisions.why: exaudíre → escutar (D3), twice running: the turn of the psalm. The Latin has a perfect (the Diurnal, from the Hebrew, a present).

options.label: escutou … escutou
options.note: D3, applied, in the Latin's tense; one slot, so the repetition cannot be broken.

options.label: ouviu … ouviu
options.note: Matos Soares 1932, Douay-Rheims 'hath heard'. audíre's verb (D3).

decisions.why: Two nouns of prayer side by side (δέησις / προσευχή). The glossary has deprecátio → súplica (open, Ps 118:58) and orátio → oração. But 'súplica' is a proparoxytone, and the noun stands at a cadence in most of its fourteen verses (grep: deprecatiónem meam closes a colon in 6:10, 16:1a, 38:13, 54:2, 60:2, 141:7; vocem deprecatiónis meæ closes one in 27:6, 65:19, 85:6, 129:2b, 139:7). Rule 4 asks for the stress on the last or second-last syllable there.

options.label: a minha prece
options.note: Ruling: a plain word of its own beside 'oração', paroxytone, of the very root of de-precári (prex). 'A voz da minha prece' will close the five cadences that 'súplica' cannot. The verb can stay 'suplicar'. Proposed for the glossary in place of the noun 'súplica'. Cost: the first colon is five syllables short of the Latin's long noun.

options.label: a minha súplica
options.note: The glossary's noun; Matos Soares 1932 and the Diurnal. Proparoxytone at the mediant (the hard checks pass it; the ear at a psalm tone does not).

decisions.why: suscípere → amparar is settled (D19) — on places where the object is a person (3:6, 117:13 Dóminus suscépit me). Here the object is a prayer, and the Greek changes verb accordingly (προσεδέξατο, 'received favourably', not ἀντελάβετο). 'O Senhor amparou a minha oração' says that he propped it up. The psalter has other such objects: 47:10 Suscépimus, Deus, misericórdiam tuam; 71:3 Suscípiant montes pacem.

options.label: acolheu
options.note: Ruling for a thing as object: to take in with favour — the Greek's sense, the Diurnal's verb ('acolhe a minha oração'), and the nearest neighbour of 'amparar' (acolher is to take under one's roof). D19 is not touched: proposed as an `open` row, suscípere with a thing as object → acolher.

options.label: recebeu
options.note: Matos Soares 1932, Douay-Rheims 'hath received'. Plain; it is accípere's verb and says less than sus-cípere.

options.label: amparou
options.note: D19's verb. Refused here: a prayer is not held up from falling; it fails outright in 47:10.

decisions.latin: Erubéscant, et conturbéntur veheménter omnes inimíci mei: * convertántur et erubéscant valde velóciter
decisions.why: The Latin opens on its verbs and brings the subject last. Draft 1 kept that; it was the stylist's worst line: the comma breaks the coordination, the late subject makes the reciter hold up an unspontaneous construction, and 'sejam grandemente perturbados' is heavy.

options.label: Que todos os meus inimigos corem e fiquem muito perturbados: * que se voltem e corem muito depressa

forms.v11a: Que todos os meus inimigos {erubescant1q} e fiquem {vehementer} {conturbentur}

options.note: Draft 2, the stylist's line: subject first under a jussive 'Que', repeated at the second colon. Order and a particle — grammar, which D2 gives to the ear; every Latin word is still there, 'corem' twice and 'perturbados' still closing the psalm's chain. 'Fiquem perturbados' for conturbéntur: still a passive participle, in the resultative form Portuguese prefers, and it answers 'estão perturbados' of 6:3. The Latin's comma after the first verb goes with the old order.

options.label: Corem, e sejam muito perturbados todos os meus inimigos: * voltem-se e corem muito depressa

forms.v11a: {erubescant1}, e sejam {vehementer} {conturbentur} todos os meus inimigos

options.note: Draft 1: the Latin's order and punctuation, the curse opening on its verb.

decisions.why: erubéscere, to redden, to blush with shame (nine verses; grep), twice in the verse. D15 gave 'ser envergonhado' to confúndi and noted that erubéscere, which stands beside it (34:4/26, 39:15, 69:3–4; 82:18 has Erubéscant … et confundántur in one verse), needs another word — 'proposed corar'. This is the first verse to meet it. The blind reader understood bare 'Corem' at once as the enemies being put to shame; the stylist rebuilt the verse but kept 'corem' twice.

options.label: Corem … corem
options.note: Ruling: D15's proposal, tried — and it holds. It is the Latin's own image — e-rubéscere is to go red — kept concrete (rule 5) and unexplained (rule 2), one word for one, and it leaves 'envergonhar' to confúndi, so 82:18 can say both. Repeated identically, as the Latin. Heard: the blind reader took it at once for shame wished on the enemies; the stylist kept 'corem' twice in his own line; the Latinist passed it.

options.label: Corem de vergonha … corem de vergonha
options.note: Unmistakable; explains the blush, brings 'vergonha' back beside confúndi's word, and the first colon runs four syllables over.

options.label: Envergonhem-se … envergonhem-se
options.note: The natural verb. Differs from confúndi → 'ser envergonhado' only in voice, and 82:18 would repeat itself.

options.label: Sejam confundidos … sejam cobertos de ignomínia
options.note: Matos Soares 1932: two renderings for the repeated verb; 'confundidos' was heard as 'confused' in Ps 118 (D15).

decisions.why: The Latin has valde in 6:4, veheménter in 6:11a and valde again in 6:11b (the Greek σφόδρα all three times). valde → muito. veheménter has seven verses (20:2 exsultábit veheménter, 103:1 magnificátus es veheménter, 118:140, 167 diléxit ea veheménter). The stylist found 'sejam grandemente perturbados' heavy in recitation and wrote 'muito'.

options.label: muito
options.note: Draft 2, from the stylist. The plainer of two faithful words (D2), and on D15's test the Latin's variation valde / veheménter carries no difference of sense: the Greek has σφόδρα all three times. A gain comes with it: 6:4 'muito perturbada' is now answered by 6:11 'muito perturbados', as the Greek answers ἐταράχθη σφόδρα with ταραχθείησαν σφόδρα. Cost: one Portuguese adverb for two Latin ones.

options.label: grandemente
options.note: Draft 1: a second adverb, because the Latin has a second; it goes with every verb the psalter gives veheménter. Refused by the stylist as heavy ('pesa na recitação').

options.label: em extremo
options.note: Matos Soares 1932 (he uses it for valde in 6:4 as well).

decisions.why: velóciter has seven verses, three of them the prayer 'velóciter exáudi me' (68:18, 101:3, 142:7a).

options.label: muito depressa
options.note: Ruling: valde → 'muito' as in 6:4, and the plain adverb; 'escutai-me depressa' will serve the three prayers. Closes on a paroxytone.

options.label: bem depressa
options.note: More idiomatic; leaves 'muito', the psalm's word for valde.

options.label: num momento
options.note: Matos Soares 1932 (the Hebrew's 'in a moment'); drops valde.

choices.6:2: The psalm begins at 6:2 (6:1 is the titulus; D7). 6:2 = 37:2 word for word (grep): Ps 37 copies this verse. furor → furor, ira → ira (glossary), in the Latin's order — furor first. The Latin fronts 'in furóre tuo' for emphasis; in Portuguese the emphasis falls at the end of the clause, so 'no vosso furor' closes the colon.
choices.6:3: 'Miserére mei' → 'Tende piedade de mim' (glossary formula). 'Dómine' twice, kept twice. 'ossa mea conturbáta sunt' returns in 30:11.
choices.6:4: 'Et' kept. valde → 'muito'. 'sed tu, Dómine, úsquequo?' → 'mas vós, Senhor, até quando?': the broken question is the Latin's and is not completed (Matos Soares adds dots and a footnote); úsquequo → 'até quando' as Ps 4:3.
choices.6:5: 'salvum me fac' → 'salvai-me' (glossary). propter → 'por causa de', as Ps 5:9 (Matos Soares 1932 'pela'). ánima mea → 'a minha alma' (glossary).
choices.6:6: 'memor esse' + genitive → 'lembrar-se de', as Ps 118:49, 52, 55. autem → 'porém'. The Latin's question mark kept. The blind reader heard 'no inferno' first as the place of eternal punishment and second as the world of the dead (decision inferno) — foreseen, and kept.
choices.6:7: The flex is kept. Tenses as the Latin: one perfect (Laborávi) and two futures (lavábo, rigábo); the Diurnal, from the Hebrew, has presents. rigáre → regar (103:13); lácrimæ → lágrimas.
choices.6:8: óculus singular → 'olho' (glossary). inveteráre → envelhecer (31:3 inveteravérunt ossa mea). 'inter omnes inimícos meos' → 'entre todos os meus inimigos'.
choices.6:9: 'omnes, qui operámini' is second person: 'todos vós que praticais' (plural humans are vós). operári iniquitátem → 'praticar a iniquidade' (glossary; as Ps 5:7a). fletus → 'pranto' (Matos Soares 1932, the Diurnal); 'vocem fletus mei' → 'a voz do meu pranto'. Second colon −3.
choices.6:10: The Latin is a chiasm (Exaudívit Dóminus … Dóminus … suscépit); Portuguese has subject–verb–object twice (D2: order yields), and 'O Senhor … o Senhor' keeps the doubled name. First colon −4: the Latin noun alone has six syllables.
choices.6:11: conturbéntur is passive: 'fiquem … perturbados' (draft 1 'sejam … perturbados'). Subject first since draft 2 (decision v11order).

Repeats found by grep over the DO Latin (ps005/grep_latin.py): 6:2 = 37:2 word for word; 6:3b 'conturbáta sunt ossa mea' ~ 30:11; 'Convértere, Dómine' + 'úsquequo' = 89:13; 'Laborávi' = 68:4; 6:9a is near 118:115. Homograph ban checked at every vós imperative: Tende, curai-me, Voltai-vos, libertai, salvai-me, Afastai-vos are all -ar/-er verbs and safe. Glossary tests this psalm was asked to make: D5 at 6:6 ('quem vos dará graças?' — holds); conturbáre → perturbar on bones, soul, eye and enemies (kept, as the psalm's frame); erubéscere → corar (D15's proposal). Departures from the glossary, each a decision: erípere → 'libertai' here ('arrancai a minha alma' is 'tear out my soul'); suscípere with a prayer as object → 'acolheu' (D19's amparar was made on persons); deprecátio → 'prece' (súplica is a proparoxytone and the noun lives at cadences).

outcomes.remark: 'Voltai-vos': turn your attention / come back; 'libertai a minha alma': from sin or damnation / from suffering or death

outcomes.remark: 'no inferno': the place of eternal punishment / the world of the dead — the first heard first

outcomes.remark: 'lavarei … o meu leito': clean it with water / soak it with weeping

outcomes.remark: 'pelo furor': my own rage / the Lord's wrath / the enemies' fury
outcomes.reason: The Latin has no possessive; the openness is kept on purpose.

outcomes.remark: 'Corem, e sejam … perturbados': a wish / an order to the enemies; 'voltem-se': retreat / turn to God / turn round
outcomes.reason: The wish was heard first; convertántur is open in the same three ways.
